string.text: Many people across the Americas trace their ancestry to Akan-speaking populations due to the trans-Atlantic slave trade. Between the 17th and 19th centuries, a significant proportion of enslaved Africans shipped from the Gold Coast—estimated at 10% of all embarkations from West Africa—were of Akan origin. Although gold remained central to the Akan economy, the intensification of internal conflicts—especially among the Fante and Ashanti during the 18th century—led to the capture and external sale of war captives, many of whom were exported through coastal ports such as Anomabo and Cape Coast.

By 1715, the Algonquin peoples of the Ottawa River Valley and adjacent regions navigated a complex, transitional landscape shaped by the aftermath of the Great Peace of Montreal in 1701 and the conclusion of Queen Anne's War in 1713. Secure from the devastating, systematic Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) raids of the previous century, Algonquin bands operated within a stabilized geopolitical framework, maintaining their traditional seasonal cycles of hunting, fishing, and gathering while expanding their pivotal role as middleman traders in the French fur trade network. However, this period of relative peace brought its own pressures; the intensified focus on the fur trade altered their traditional subsistence economy, increased their reliance on European trade goods, and accelerated cultural changes as Catholic missions, such as those at Sillery and later Lake of the Two Mountains, concentrated populations and deeply influenced local social structures.

By 1715, the British colonies in North America were experiencing a period of rapid demographic growth and economic consolidation following the conclusion of Queen Anne's War. Divided into three distinct regions—the farming and maritime-focused New England colonies, the ethnically diverse agricultural Middle colonies, and the plantation-dominated Southern colonies—they were increasingly bound together by the transatlantic slave trade and mercantilist policies. While individual colonies maintained localized assemblies and distinct religious foundations, the expansion of commercial networks and a shared reliance on British manufacturing were subtly binding them to the British Empire. Concurrently, the brutal expansion of the plantation economy, particularly via the escalating importation of enslaved Africans, entrenched deep racial hierarchies that would fundamentally shape the socio-political landscape of the continent for centuries to come.

The Iroquoian peoples are an ethnolinguistic group of peoples from eastern North America. Their traditional territories, often referred to by scholars as Iroquoia, stretch from the mouth of the St. Lawrence River in the north, to modern-day North Carolina in the south. Historical Iroquoian people were the Five nations of the Iroquois or Haudenosaunee, Huron or Wendat, Petun, Neutral or Attawandaron, Erie people, Wenro, Susquehannock and the St. Lawrence Iroquoians.

Between the 9th and 15th centuries, Bantu-speaking states began to emerge in the Great Lakes region and in the savanna south of the Central African rainforests. The Monomotapa kings built the Great Zimbabwe complex, a civilisation ancestral to the Shona people. Toward the 18th and 19th centuries, the flow of Zanj slaves from Southeast Africa increased with the rise of the Sultanate of Zanzibar. With the arrival of European colonialists, the Zanzibar Sultanate came into direct trade conflict and competition with Portuguese and other Europeans along the Swahili Coast, leading eventually to the fall of the Sultanate and the end of slave trading on the Swahili Coast in the mid-20th century.

The Muscogee, also known as the Mvskoke, Muscogee Creek or just Creek, are a group of related Indigenous peoples of the Southeastern Woodlands in the United States. Their historical homelands are in what now comprises southern Tennessee, much of Alabama, western Georgia and parts of northern Florida.

The Pirate Republic or Republic of Pirates refers to a period in the early 18th century when pirates established a self-governed, albeit informal, republic in Nassau, Bahamas. This period, during the Golden Age of Piracy, saw pirates operating with a degree of autonomy, governed by a pirate code and democratic principles within their crews.

The Sioux have two major linguistic divisions, the Dakota and Lakota peoples. Collectively, they are the Očhéthi Šakówiŋ, or 'Seven Council Fires'. The term Sioux, an exonym from a French transcription of the Ojibwe term Nadowessi, can refer to any ethnic group within the Great Sioux Nation or to any of the nation's many language dialects. Before the 17th century, the Santee Dakota lived around Lake Superior with territories in present-day northern Minnesota and Wisconsin. They gathered wild rice, hunted woodland animals, and used canoes to fish. Wars with the Ojibwe throughout the 18th century pushed the Dakota west into southern Minnesota, where the Western Dakota (Yankton, Yanktonai) and Lakota (Teton) lived.
